issues.legal_issue: An appeal lies to a Division Bench from a Single Judge’s order in a company-affairs proceeding where the applicable appeal provision directs appeals to the same court.
material_facts: The appellant brought a proceeding concerning the company’s affairs under provisions for relief against oppression and mismanagement and interim orders.
The Single Judge determined the parties’ liabilities under their compromise.
The appellant appealed to the Division Bench, which dismissed the appeal on the ground that no Letters Patent or other provision provided for it.
issues.conclusion: The appeal lay to the Division Bench under section 483 of the Companies Act, 1956, and the Division Bench was wrong to dismiss it for want of an applicable Letters Patent provision.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 397 and 398 read with section 403, and section 483 of the Companies Act, 1956, support an appeal to the same court in the same manner as other appeals within its ordinary jurisdiction; an appeal from a Single Judge therefore lies to the Division Bench. The Court followed Shankarlal Aggarwal v. S.L. Poddar, AIR 1965 SC 507, and relied on Shanta Genevienve Pommerat v. Papers Pvt. Ltd., AIR 1983 SC 269; M/s. Golcha Investment (P) Ltd. v. Shanti Chandra Bafna, AIR 1970 SC 1350; and M/s. Tarapose & Co. v. Cochin Shipyard Ltd., AIR 1984 SC 1072.

predicates.company_affairs_proceeding: The proceeding seeks relief concerning the affairs of a company.
predicates.single_judge_order: A Single Judge makes an order in that proceeding.
predicates.statutory_appeal_to_same_court: The applicable appeal provision directs an appeal to the same court as appeals from other orders within its ordinary jurisdiction.

issues.definition: When a Single Judge makes an order in a company-affairs proceeding and the applicable appeal provision directs appeals to the same court, an appeal lies to that court’s Division Bench.

issues.legal_issue: The absence of procedural rules does not defeat a statutory right to appeal or the High Court’s jurisdiction to hear that appeal.
material_facts: The appeal was brought from a Single Judge’s decision, but the High Court had no applicable procedural rules for filing and disposing of that type of appeal.
The High Court had treated the absence of an applicable Letters Patent provision as a reason that no appeal lay.
issues.conclusion: The absence of procedural rules does not take away the litigant’s right to file an appeal conferred by statute or the High Court’s jurisdiction to dispose of it; the High Court should frame rules under its rule-making power.
issues.legal_principle: Where a statute confers a right of appeal, procedural rules govern its exercise but their absence does not extinguish the right or the court’s jurisdiction. The Court relied on the principles in Shankarlal Aggarwal v. S.L. Poddar, AIR 1965 SC 507, and M/s. Golcha Investment (P) Ltd. v. Shanti Chandra Bafna, AIR 1970 SC 1350.

predicates.appeal_from_single_judge_order: A litigant seeks to appeal a Single Judge’s order.
predicates.statutory_appeal_right: The governing law confers a right to appeal that order.
predicates.procedural_rules_absent: The court has no procedural rules for filing or disposing of that appeal.

issues.definition: If a litigant appeals a Single Judge’s order, the law confers an appeal right, and procedural rules are absent, the appeal right remains and the High Court may hear the appeal.

issues.legal_issue: The liability determination under a compromise should give effect to the compromise’s specified debt terms, the agreed sharing of liabilities, and payments made.
material_facts: The parties agreed that company liabilities would be shared equally and specified the amount of a particular bank liability in their compromise.
After the parties could not agree on an auditor, they agreed that the court would determine liability by reference to the balance sheet and the payments made by each party.

The Division Bench used the specified amount for the bank liability rather than the higher amount shown for it in the balance sheet, considered the appellant’s post-compromise payment, and fixed the appellant’s remaining liability.
The appellant challenged the Division Bench’s computation and sought a further credit for the payment already made.
issues.conclusion: The Court upheld the Division Bench’s computation and directed the appellant to pay the resulting balance in settlement of the dues.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the terms of the parties’ compromise and the agreed basis for determining liabilities, including the specified bank-liability figure and the parties’ payments. No statutory provision or earlier case was relied on for this computation.

rule.if: company_liability_appeal and settlement_specified_debt_component and settlement_required_equal_sharing and liability_based_on_agreed_accounts and payments_considered

predicates.company_liability_appeal: An appeal challenges a court’s determination of liabilities arising from a company settlement.
predicates.settlement_specified_debt_component: The parties’ settlement specified the amount of a particular debt component.
predicates.settlement_required_equal_sharing: The parties’ settlement required them to share liabilities equally.
predicates.liability_based_on_agreed_accounts: The parties agreed that liability would be determined using identified accounts or balance sheets.
predicates.payments_considered: The court considered payments made by a party when determining that party’s liability.

issues.definition: In an appeal concerning company liabilities, when the settlement specifies a debt component, requires equal sharing, fixes an accounting basis, and the court considers payments made, the settlement-based liability determination is upheld.
